passage: The school's eco club met every Wednesday in the science lab. This week, Mahima, a Class 6 girl, brought a surprising chart. She had checked every tap in the girls' washroom for a week. "Three drip all day," she said. "I held a bottle under one. It filled in one lunch break." Arnab, who ran the club, whistled. Their teacher asked what they could do. Mahima had a list ready: write to the caretaker, put little signs above the sinks, and switch off the corridor fans at break. Arnab added, "And we check again next month." Two weeks later, the caretaker fixed the taps. Mahima drew a small smiling tap on the sign 🙂.

qa.q: How many taps in the girls' washroom dripped all day?
qa.a: Three taps dripped all day.

qa.q: What does Mahima's list suggest about how she felt about the dripping taps?
qa.a: It suggests she was bothered by the waste and determined to fix it, since she tested it for a week and came with ready steps.

qa.q: Why was Arnab's idea to check again next month useful?
qa.a: It turns one action into a habit and lets the club see whether the changes, like signs and switching off fans, actually keep working.

qa.q: How might the caretaker see the children's letter?
qa.a: He might be glad someone noticed and reported the problem clearly, or at first feel it was more work, but the fixed taps show he took it seriously.

grounding: It shows children in a school club noticing water and energy waste and taking practical steps to reduce it.

passage: My cousin Pooja is staying with us for the holidays, and my sister Mehak, who is nine, has turned into the house's light police. Pooja and I noticed it on the first day. Mehak walked behind Papa switching off the fan he'd left on. She put a bucket under the AC drip and used that water for the tulsi plant. When Pooja threw a half-full water bottle in the bin, Mehak fished it out, poured the water into the plant pot and said nothing. Pooja looked embarrassed. Later Mehak made a chart on the fridge with ticks for every switch turned off. I don't know if she learned it at school or just decided it herself. She won't say. 😅

qa.q: What did Mehak use the AC drip water for?
qa.a: She used it to water the tulsi plant.

qa.q: Why might Pooja have looked embarrassed?
qa.a: Mehak silently took out her half-full bottle and used the water, so Pooja probably realised she had wasted it and felt a little caught out.

qa.q: What could the family do to support Mehak's habits without making guests uncomfortable?
qa.a: They could join her fridge chart as a family game, so saving water and power feels shared rather than like someone checking on others.

qa.q: How might Papa see Mehak switching off the fan behind him?
qa.a: He might find it funny or a bit annoying at first, but it could also remind him to switch it off himself.

grounding: An older sibling describes a child building everyday habits to save water and electricity at home.

passage:
Week one: At the summer camp in Lisbon, Kishore's cabin threw away three bags of plastic cups in two days. Maria, their leader, held up one bag. "All this, in two days?" Kishore shrugged. Everyone did it.

Week two: Maria gave each camper a metal mug with a sticker for their name. Kishore lost his on the second day and had to ask for a paper cup. He hated being the only one. He found the mug under the bench and wrote his name again in marker.

Week three: The cabin bin held one small bag. Kishore reminded a younger boy, "Use your mug, not the cups," and felt a little proud of saying it.

qa.q: What did Maria give each camper in week two?
qa.a: She gave each camper a metal mug with a name sticker.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel when he had to ask for a paper cup?
qa.a: He hated being the only one using it, which shows he felt awkward and had started caring about fitting the new habit.

qa.q: What made the change work across the three weeks?
qa.a: Maria made the waste visible, gave an easy alternative, and let the habit grow until the campers reminded each other.

qa.q: What would change if Maria had only lectured the cabin about plastic?
qa.a: Without the mugs and seeing the bags, Kishore might have kept shrugging, since he had no simple way to change what everyone did.

grounding: It shows a child changing a wasteful habit over three weeks into a small waste-reducing routine.

passage: Nandini, come here and close that tap first. Good. Now, when I was your age in Bikaner, water came in a tanker twice a week. My mother kept every drop in brass pots. We bathed with one bucket, and the bath water went to the tulsi and the neem. Dishwater went to the chillies. Once I spilt a whole pot playing, and I cried, because I knew what it meant. So I became the water guard of our house. I scolded my brothers if they let the tap drip at the neighbour's. Here the water comes from a pipe, so you forget. But it doesn't grow in the pipe, beta. Shall we put a mug under the RO waste tomorrow, for mopping?

qa.q: How often did water come to the narrator's childhood home in Bikaner?
qa.a: It came in a tanker twice a week.

qa.q: Why did the narrator cry as a child after spilling a pot?
qa.a: The narrator understood how precious that water was for the family and felt guilty for wasting it.

qa.q: What small step does the narrator suggest to Nandini?
qa.a: Putting a mug under the RO waste pipe so the water can be used for mopping.

qa.q: How might Nandini see water differently after this story?
qa.a: Nandini might start noticing running taps and realise water isn't endless just because it comes easily.

grounding: An elder recalls childhood water-saving habits and passes a small daily habit on to a child.

passage: That May, the building's water came for only one hour each morning, and Yash, eleven, was put in charge of making it last. At six he and his little sister Aadhya filled every bucket and bottle in the flat, yawning. 'Rules,' Yash announced, writing on the fridge. 'Tap off while brushing. One mug of water for washing hands, not running water. Vegetable water goes to the plants.' Aadhya pointed at the ceiling fan whirring in the empty room. 'That's electricity, not water.' 'Still wasting,' said Yash, and switched it off. By the fourth day, two buckets were left over. Papa noticed. 'Did we get extra water?' 'No,' said Aadhya proudly. 'Yash made rules.'

qa.q: How long did the building get water each morning?
qa.a: Only one hour each morning.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel when Papa asked about extra water?
qa.a: She felt proud of the rules and of the buckets they had saved together.

qa.q: Which of Yash's rules could any family try?
qa.a: Turning the tap off while brushing, using a mug for handwashing and giving vegetable water to plants.

qa.q: What would change if the water came all day again?
qa.a: Yash and Aadhya might slip back into careless habits unless they kept the rules going anyway.

grounding: Shows a child saving water and energy at home under a water shortage.

passage:
In their Delhi flat, Tarun, ten, stuck two labels on two buckets under the sink: WET and DRY.
His sister Sarika laughed. “You think Mummy will use them?”
“She will if I help.”
Every evening after dinner, Tarun checked the buckets. Peels in wet, wrappers in dry. He took the wet one down to the colony's compost pit on Sundays.
He also started turning off the tap while brushing and switching off the fan when he left a room.
After a month, the family's dustbin bags went from two a day to one. Sarika started using the buckets too, without saying anything.

qa.q: What labels did Tarun stick on the buckets?
qa.a: WET and DRY.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel when Sarika laughed at his idea?
qa.a: He felt determined, sure it would work if he helped.

qa.q: Which of Tarun's habits reduced waste, and how?
qa.a: Sorting wet and dry waste and composting peels, which cut the dustbin bags from two a day to one.

qa.q: How does Sarika's attitude change?
qa.a: She starts out laughing but later quietly uses the buckets too.

grounding: A ten-year-old starts habits to reduce waste and save water and energy at home.

passage:
“Yash, you've left the fan on in your room again.”
“I'm coming back!”
“In an hour?” Hansa, eleven, switched it off. “Every day the lights are on in rooms nobody's in.”
“So? Papa pays the bill.”
“It's not just money. It uses power from coal. Our teacher showed us.”
Yash rolled his eyes. “Okay, Miss Environment.”
“Let's make a chart. Every room, every switch. Whoever leaves one on does the dishes.”
“Deal. But you'll lose first.”
By the weekend, Hansa had done the dishes once, and Yash three times. But the lights were off.

qa.q: What did Hansa suggest as a penalty?
qa.a: Whoever leaves a switch on does the dishes.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel about the lights left on?
qa.a: She felt annoyed and concerned about wasting power.

qa.q: Why was the chart a clever idea?
qa.a: It turned saving energy into a fun family game with a clear rule.

qa.q: How does Yash see Hansa's idea at first?
qa.a: He sees it as fussy, calling her Miss Environment, but agrees to play.

grounding: An eleven-year-old helps her family save energy with a fun switch-off chart.

passage:
I noticed it on Sports Day: a mountain of plastic water bottles in the bins behind the ground. Hundreds.
I'm Simran. I told my friend Hafsa, “We should do something.” She said, “What can two Class 6 kids do?”
We made a poster: BRING YOUR OWN BOTTLE. We asked the principal if the school could put a water filter near the ground. She agreed.
For the next Sports Day, everyone was asked to bring a steel bottle. Hafsa and I stood by the filter handing out stickers to anyone who did.
The bins were almost empty afterwards. Hafsa said, “Okay, two kids can do something.”

qa.q: What did the poster say?
qa.a: BRING YOUR OWN BOTTLE.

qa.q: How did Simran feel on seeing the mountain of plastic bottles?
qa.a: Simran felt upset and motivated to do something.

qa.q: What steps made the bottle drive work?
qa.a: A poster, asking the principal for a water filter, and handing out stickers to reward steel bottles.

qa.q: How does Hafsa's view change?
qa.a: Hafsa starts doubtful and ends convinced that two kids can make a difference.

grounding: A student starts a school drive to reduce plastic bottle waste.

passage:
Class 6 teacher's note.
Deepak noticed that our classroom fans and lights stay on during PE and lunch, when the room is empty. He told me, a bit annoyed: "It's a waste."
I asked what he'd suggest. He and Jahnavi made a rota: two "energy monitors" each week who switch off before leaving. Jahnavi made a sign for the door: "Last out? Lights out!"
This week, the room has been dark every lunchtime. Other classes have started asking about it.
Next, they want to count how many taps drip in the school and report it to the office. I've said yes. — Mrs Pillai

qa.q: What sign did Jahnavi make for the door?
qa.a: "Last out? Lights out!"

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when he told the teacher about the fans?
qa.a: Deepak felt annoyed about the waste and wanted something done.

qa.q: What did Mrs Pillai do that helped Deepak act?
qa.a: She asked for his suggestion instead of just agreeing, which let him and Jahnavi make their own plan.

qa.q: How might other classes see Deepak and Jahnavi's rota?
qa.a: They seem curious and may want to copy it in their own rooms.

grounding: A teacher notes children starting an energy-saving routine in class.

passage:
Dear Diary,
The tap in our bathroom has been dripping for a week. Tonight I put a bucket under it before bed.
This morning — the bucket was almost half full! From one drip!
I showed Hafsa from next door. She said, "That's so much water, just going down the drain."
So I used the bucket water to water our plants and wash the balcony. Then I told Papa, and he called the plumber.
Also, I'm going to take bucket baths now instead of the shower. Hafsa laughed and said, "You'll give up in two days."
We'll see. I'm Manoj, and I'm stubborn.

qa.q: How full was the bucket in the morning?
qa.a: Almost half full.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when seeing the half-full bucket?
qa.a: Manoj felt shocked and surprised at how much water the drip wasted.

qa.q: What steps did Manoj take that anyone could copy?
qa.a: Manoj reused the bucket water, told Papa so the tap got fixed, and decided to take bucket baths.

qa.q: How does Hafsa see Manoj's plan?
qa.a: Hafsa doubts Manoj will keep it up and teases about giving up in two days.

grounding: In a diary a child discovers how much water a dripping tap wastes and takes action.

passage:
The morning after the village fair, the ground was covered with plastic cups, wrappers and plates. Cows were nosing through them.
Mahima frowned. "They'll eat plastic."
Anjali grabbed a sack from her father's shop. "Let's pick it up."
They started with the cups. Other kids came to watch. A few joined.
By noon, they had four sacks full. Mahima separated the leaf plates. "These can go in the compost pit."
The sarpanch saw them and came over. "Who told you to do this?"
"Nobody," said Anjali. "The cows."
He laughed and promised dustbins for the next fair.

qa.q: How many sacks did the children fill by noon?
qa.a: Four sacks.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when she saw the cows nosing through the waste?
qa.a: Mahima felt worried that the cows would eat plastic.

qa.q: Which of the children's actions cut down the waste?
qa.a: They cleaned up, separated leaf plates for compost, and their effort got the sarpanch to promise dustbins.

qa.q: How might the sarpanch see the children's work?
qa.a: The sarpanch is impressed and amused, and it pushes him to plan better for the next fair.

grounding: Village children clean up after a fair and separate compostable waste.

passage:
In Nairobi the water came only on Tuesdays and Fridays that month, and Amara's family filled every jerrycan. Her friend Yuki, whose family had just moved from Osaka, came over after school and turned on the kitchen tap to wash one cup.
"Stop!" Amara laughed, grabbing it. "That's tomorrow's cooking water."
Yuki went pink. "Sorry. In our old flat it never stopped."
Amara showed her the system: a bowl in the sink for washing, then that water goes to the plants; the rinse water flushes the toilet. Yuki started counting how many cups they used.
The next week Yuki came with a drawing of her own family's kitchen, with a new bowl in the sink and an arrow to their balcony plants.

qa.q: On which days did the water come that month?
qa.a: The water came only on Tuesdays and Fridays.

qa.q: Why did Yuki go pink?
qa.a: Yuki felt embarrassed about wasting water without thinking, because it had never been scarce for her before.

qa.q: Which part of Amara's system could any family copy, and why?
qa.a: Reusing the washing bowl water for plants, because it's simple and saves water without extra cost.

qa.q: How might Amara feel when Yuki brings the drawing?
qa.a: Amara probably feels pleased and a little proud that her family's habits helped a friend change hers.

grounding: Shows children learning and spreading everyday water-saving habits.

passage:
It was May and the school felt like an oven, but when Zainab and Yamini walked past Class 6C at lunch, all four fans and the lights were on in an empty room.
"Every day," Zainab said. "Same in 6A."
They made a checklist on chart paper: fans off, lights off, taps closed. Each class would get a "last one out" monitor. Yamini drew a sweating sun on it so people would read it.
The first week, nobody bothered. The second week, Yamini went round at lunch and quietly switched things off herself. The third week, the headmistress read their chart aloud at assembly.
By June, 6C's monitor was the one reminding Zainab to switch off.

qa.q: What did Zainab and Yamini see in empty Class 6C at lunch?
qa.a: All four fans and the lights were on in an empty room.

qa.q: How do you think Yamini felt when nobody followed the checklist the first week?
qa.a: Yamini was likely disappointed and a bit frustrated, but determined, since she started switching things off herself.

qa.q: What went right in the third week that could help other schools?
qa.a: The headmistress backing the chart at assembly, because students take a habit more seriously when adults support it.

qa.q: How might the 6C monitor see the job by June?
qa.a: The monitor seems to feel responsible and proud, even reminding Zainab, the chart's own maker, to switch off.

grounding: Illustrates children starting an energy-saving habit in school during a hot season.

passage:
I'm Anand, from the flat across the landing. This Diwali I noticed Naveen doing strange things.
When gifts came, Naveen didn't tear the wrapping. Naveen folded it flat and put it in a box marked "next year". The sweets came in plastic trays; Naveen washed them and took them down to the aunty who sells flowers, for her marigolds.
On Diwali night the whole building was blazing. At midnight, Naveen went out and switched their string lights off, leaving just the clay diyas burning. I asked why.
"Lights on all night for nobody," Naveen said. "The diyas are prettier anyway."
I can't tell if Naveen is doing it for the planet or just likes order. But this year, our landing had a box for folded paper too. 🪔

qa.q: What did Naveen do with the plastic sweet trays?
qa.a: Naveen washed them and took them down to the aunty who sells flowers, for her marigolds.

qa.q: What does Naveen's answer about the lights suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Naveen was bothered by the waste but content with less, enjoying the diyas more than the blazing string lights.

qa.q: How could Naveen's family build on these habits?
qa.a: They could make the reuse box and the midnight switch-off a shared family routine, not just Naveen's.

qa.q: Why might Anand be unsure of Naveen's reasons?
qa.a: Anand is only watching from across the landing, so Anand can see the actions but not know what Naveen really thinks.

grounding: Shows, through a neighbour's eyes, a child reducing waste and saving energy during a festival.

passage:
Monday: the April heat arrived early, and the tap in Rukmini's colony ran for only one hour. Her sister Nandini left the tap open while brushing her teeth. Rukmini watched the water run and said nothing.
Wednesday: Amma filled only two buckets. Rukmini, eleven, put a mug by the basin. "Brush with the mug. Not the tap." Nandini complained. Rukmini also switched off the fan in the empty room and started a box for plastic wrappers.
The next Saturday, the colony notice said the tanker would be late. Their buckets were still half full. Nandini, filling the mug, said, "Okay, your mug idea was good." Rukmini grinned and added a new rule to the fridge: "Lights off when you leave."

qa.q: How long did the tap run in Rukmini's colony?
qa.a: The tap ran for only one hour.

qa.q: What was Rukmini likely feeling when she watched the water run on Monday?
qa.a: She was likely uneasy and worried, seeing water wasted in a week of shortage, but not yet sure what to say.

qa.q: What small steps worked for the family, and why?
qa.a: Brushing with a mug, switching off the fan in empty rooms and collecting wrappers worked, because they saved water and power without big changes.

qa.q: How does Nandini's attitude change over the week?
qa.a: Nandini first complains, but when the tanker is late and the buckets are still half full, she admits the mug idea was good.

grounding: Shows a child building everyday habits to save water and energy and reduce waste during a hot summer.
